subject: Civil Engineering
title: Flexible Pavements: Asphalt Roads
description: Learn Flexible Pavements: Asphalt Roads in one minute.

hook.text: Asphalt covers 94% of paved roads in the United States. It's the world's road surface.

buildup.text: Flexible pavements bend under load. Layers of asphalt, base, and subbase spread the force.

discovery.text: Asphalt is aggregate glued together with bitumen — a petroleum product. It's recyclable.

twist.text: Hot-mix asphalt is placed at 300°F. Warm-mix uses lower temperatures to save energy.

climax.text: Perpetual pavements are designed to last 50+ years — deep layers never crack.

punchline.text: Asphalt bends, heals, and recycles. That's why it covers the world.

quiz.question: Why are asphalt pavements called 'flexible'?
options: They can be easily removed and replaced overnight
They bend slightly under traffic loads and distribute force through layers
They change color with temperature to warn drivers of ice

details.summary: Flexible pavements use layers of asphalt concrete over granular base and subbase courses to distribute traffic loads to the subgrade soil. The asphalt surface deforms slightly under each wheel load and recovers.
details.whyItMatters: Asphalt pavements carry over 90% of the world's paved roads because they are economical to build, easily maintained, and 100% recyclable. Understanding their behavior is fundamental to transportation engineering.
takeaways: Flexible pavements distribute loads through a cone of stress to underlying soil
Hot mix asphalt combines graded aggregate with bituminous binder at about 150 degrees Celsius
Pavement layers must be thick enough to reduce subgrade stress below failure limits

faq.question: Why are asphalt pavements called flexible?
faq.answer: Asphalt concrete bends and deforms slightly under each wheel load, then rebounds. This flexibility distributes stress gradually through successive layers rather than spanning across them like rigid concrete.

faq.question: What causes rutting in asphalt pavements?
faq.answer: Rutting occurs when heavy wheel loads permanently deform the asphalt or underlying layers. In hot weather, asphalt binder softens, allowing aggregate to shift under repeated loads. Weak subgrade soil can also deform, creating wider and deeper ruts visible at the surface.
